en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Second Chapter
The Discourse on Causing Others to Transcend:
Is there causing others to transcend for an arahant?
Yes, there is.
Is it not the case that an Arahant is led by others, dependent on others, reliant on others, bound to others, and thus neither knows nor sees, being confused and lacking clear comprehension?
One should certainly not say this... [etc.

... Is it not rather the case that an Arahant is not led by others, not dependent on others, not reliant on others, not bound to others, and thus knows and sees, being unconfused and possessing clear comprehension?
“Yes.

“If it is so that an Arahant is not led by others, does not rely on others, does not depend on others, and is not bound to others, and he knows and sees, undeluded and clearly comprehending, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘There is in an Arahant the causing of others to understand.’”

Is it the case that an ordinary person (puthujjana) has guidance from others, and he is led by others, dependent on others, reliant on others, and bound to others, such that he does not know, does not see, is deluded, and lacks clear comprehension?
Yes, it is.

Is it the case that an Arhat has guidance from others, and he is led by others, dependent on others, reliant on others, and bound to others, such that he does not know, does not see, is deluded, and lacks clear comprehension?

It should not be said thus … [as before] … Does the Arahant have the quality of leading others across, and is he himself not led by others, not dependent on others, not conditioned by others, not bound to others, but knows and sees, undeluded and with full awareness? Yes.

Is it the case that an ordinary person (puthujjana) has been led by another, yet he is not led by others, does not follow others, does not rely on others, and is not dependent on others, but knows and sees, undeluded and with full awareness?
One should not say so… [as before]… Is it the case that an Arhat has been led by another?
“Yes,” he said. “An arahant has encouragement regarding the Teacher, encouragement regarding the Dhamma, encouragement regarding the Saṅgha, encouragement regarding the training,
encouragement regarding the past, encouragement regarding the future, and encouragement regarding both the past and the future.”
Is there an imparting by another regarding the phenomena that are dependently originated through specific conditionality?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...

There is no imparting by another for an Arahant regarding the Teacher, nor regarding the Dhamma... [and so on] ... Is there an imparting by another regarding the phenomena that are dependently originated through specific conditionality?
“Yes.

“If it is admitted that there is no instigating others by an Arahant regarding the Teacher, nor regarding the Dhamma … [and so on] … nor regarding the phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality (idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppanna), then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘There is instigating others by an Arahant.’”

Is there, for an ordinary person (puthujjana), reliance on others regarding the Teacher, reliance on others regarding the Dhamma, and so forth … up to reliance on others regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination?
Yes.

Is there, for an Arhat, reliance on others regarding the Teacher, reliance on others regarding the Dhamma, and so forth … up to reliance on others regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … There is dependence on others for an Arahant;

there is no dependence on others regarding the Teacher, but there is dependence on others regarding the Dhamma … [as before] … and dependence on others regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination? Yes.

Is there guidance by another for an ordinary person, but no guidance by another for him regarding the Teacher, regarding the Dhamma, ... [and so on] ... regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions?
One should not say so...
Is there guidance by another for an Arahant?
“Yes.
“But is it not the case that for an Arahant, lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future?
“Yes.”

If, for an Arahant, lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future, then surely it should not be said:
"An Arahant has the power to incite others.
Is it the case that an Arahant has the power to incite others?
“Yes,” he said.
“Is it not the case that for an Arahant, hatred has been abandoned … pe … delusion has been abandoned … pe …?”
Fearlessness of wrongdoing has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future...
the path has been developed for the abandoning of lust...
the factors of enlightenment have been developed...
The path has been developed for the abandoning of hatred …pe… the path has been developed for the abandoning of lack of moral dread …pe… the factors of enlightenment have been developed …pe…
Is it not the case that the Arahant is one who is free from lust, free from hatred,
and free from delusion … [as before] … and has realized what ought to be realized?
Yes, it is.
If an Arahant—one who is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion, who has realized what is to be realized—then indeed, it should not be said:
"There is in an Arahant the leading of others across.
Is there, then, in an Arahant the leading of others across?
An arahant skilled in his own doctrine possesses the ability to refute others; an arahant skilled in other doctrines does not possess the ability to refute others.
[Is it true that] an arahant skilled in his own doctrine possesses the ability to refute others?
Yes, it is.
Does the Arahant who is skilled in other doctrines possess the quality of instructing others?
One should not say so… [as before] … Does the Arahant who is skilled in other doctrines not possess the quality of instructing others?
“Yes.
“Then it must be said that for an Arahant skilled in his own Dhamma there is no further instruction by others?
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Is lust abandoned by an Arahant skilled in his own Dhamma, and does he possess the ability to communicate it to others?
Yes. Is lust abandoned by an Arahant skilled in another’s Dhamma, and does he possess the ability to communicate it to others? Yes.
It should not be said so.
For an arahant skilled in his own Dhamma, hatred has been abandoned … pe … delusion has been abandoned … pe.
Lack of moral dread has been abandoned … the path for the abandoning of lust has been developed … the factors of enlightenment have been developed … [and so on].
The path has been developed for the abandoning of hatred …pe… the path has been developed for the abandoning of lack of moral dread …pe… the factors of enlightenment have been developed …pe…
Is it the case that for an arahant— one skilled in the Dhamma, free from lust, free from hatred,
and free from delusion … [as before] … who has realized what is to be realized— there is the capacity to lead others across?
Yes, it is.
“Is it the case that for an Arahant, skilled in the supreme Dhamma, free from lust, free from hatred,

free from delusion … [as before] … who has realized what ought to be realized, there is the further task of making others realize? “One should not say so” … [as before] … “It is impossible, it cannot occur, that such a person should have the further task of making others realize.”
Is passion abandoned by an arahant skilled in the supreme Dhamma, and does he have no further need for instruction from others?
Yes. Is passion abandoned by an arahant skilled in his own Dhamma, and does he have no further need for instruction from others? Yes.
It should not be said so.
For an Arahant skilled in the Dhamma of others, hatred has been abandoned, delusion has been abandoned …pe… lack of moral dread has been abandoned …pe….
The path has been developed for the abandoning of lust … [and] the factors of enlightenment have been developed … [likewise] for the abandoning of hatred … etc.
The path has been developed for the abandoning of fearlessness of wrongdoing … the factors of enlightenment have been developed … [and so on] … the Arahant,
free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion, is skilled in the doctrines of others … [and so on].
"Is that which is to be realized already realized, such that there is nothing further for him to be taught by another?
"Yes.
"An Arahant who is skilled in his own doctrine, free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion ... [as before] ..."
"What is to be realized has been realized; there is nothing further for him to be made to realize by another"—is this not so?
One should not say so... [etc.
...Does the Arahant have anything further to be made to realize by another?
“Yes, [it is so].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see’?”
“And what, bhikkhus, does one know and see so that the destruction of the taints occurs? ‘Such is form,’ ...pe...
‘such is the passing away of consciousness’—it is by knowing thus and seeing thus, bhikkhus, that the destruction of the taints occurs.”
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“There is instigation by another in the case of an Arahant.
Is there instigation by another in the case of an Arahant? Yes.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.
And what, bhikkhus, is it that one must know and see for the destruction of the taints to occur? ‘This is suffering’—”
Monks, for one who knows and sees, there is the destruction of the taints:

‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’— for one who knows and sees thus, there is the destruction of the taints.
“Thus, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the destruction of the taints.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said:
"There is instigation by another in an Arahant.
Is there instigation by another in an Arahant?
“Yes, [it is so].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, without directly knowing, without fully understanding, without becoming dispassionate toward, and without abandoning everything, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering’?”
“And indeed, bhikkhus, one who directly knows, fully understands, fades away toward, and abandons everything is capable of the destruction of suffering.
Is this a sutta? Yes.
In that case, it should not be said:
"There is instigation by another in an Arahant.
Is there instigation by another in an Arahant?
“Yes. [The opponent asks: “Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘Simultaneously with his attainment of vision...’?”
“The six impossibilities cannot be done.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
In that case, it should not be said:
"There is instigation by another in an Arahant.
Is there instigation by another in an Arahant?
“Yes, [it is so].
“Was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arises in a noble disciple—’?”
“Bhikkhus, with the arising of the vision that ‘whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation,’ three fetters are abandoned in a noble disciple:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes,” [he replies].
“In that case, it should not be said:
‘There is, for an Arahant, the causing of others to cross over.’”
Is there an instigation by others for an Arahant?
Yes. But was it not said by the Blessed One: [as follows]?
“I will not tolerate anyone in the world who wavers, O Dhota;
for I have fully realized the supreme Dhamma.”
“In this way you shall cross over this flood.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said:
"There is instigation by another in the case of an arahant.
It should not be said.
“Is there an Arahant’s being led across by others?”—Yes, you say.

But surely others might lead an Arahant across regarding the names and clans of men and women; others might lead him across regarding what is the path and what is not the path; and others might lead him across regarding the names of grass, wood, and forest trees?
“Yes,” he said.

“If it were so that others could cause an Arahant to forget the names and clans of men and women, or cause him to forget the right and wrong paths, or cause him to forget the names of grasses, wood, and forest trees, then indeed it would have to be said:
‘There is causing an Arahant to forget by others.’”

"Could others cause the name and clan of an Arahant to be forgotten? Could others cause him to forget the path or the non-path? Could others cause him to forget the names of grasses, sticks, or forest trees? Thus, is there such a thing as being caused to forget by another for an Arahant?
"Yes.
"Could others cause an Arahant to forget the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arahantship?"
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … The discussion on causing others to cross over is finished.
